title: KV spillback and prefix collisions - Aurora Systems technical deep dive
summary: Deep technical session focused on repeated KV cache evictions under bursty long-context workloads. Covered paging/spillback behavior, prefix reuse causing thrashing, batching impacts, and tradeoffs for 8-bit quantized models in Aurora's private VPC deployment. Agreed next steps: collect heap/kv telemetry, run targeted bench with pinned prefixes, and share runbook + config patch for cache sizing.
next_steps: Redwood to share KV debug runbook and eviction tracing guide (Liam) - due 2025-12-05
Aurora to run pinned-prefix benchmark and upload logs to shared folder - due 2025-12-09
Schedule follow-up benchmark review (30m) w/ perf graphs - target 2025-12-11
action_items: Liam O'Rourke - provide heap + kv cache sampling script and example traces by 2025-12-05
Ravi Patel - run 3 benchmark runs with long-context (8k) and pinned prefixes, upload results by 2025-12-09
Maya Chen - send pricing note for Dedicated pool with increased cache RAM options by 2025-12-06
Selena Ortiz - enable extra telemetry flags on staging private deployment and notify SE when ready
Marco Liu - confirm data residency/KMS questions in email thread by 2025-12-07
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-02
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Rourke (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (Aurora Lead ML Infra), Selena Ortiz (Aurora Platform Eng), Marco Liu (Aurora Data Privacy)

[00:00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. we want to dive into the kv cache activity you've been seeing. luke to start, but uh r- ravi, can you quickly summarize what you saw this week?
[00:00:18] Ravi: yeah sure, sorry i'm on a bit of a lag here. basically we hit a series of spikes when long context jobs (6k-8k) overlapped with a lot of small prefix-heavy requests. the runtime started evicting prefixes and we saw paging to disk — which caused latency to trip from ~120ms to 1.2s for tail requests.
[00:00:45] Selena: just to add, it's a private vpc deployment with dedicated gpus, we've got 256GB host RAM for the runtime layer but the kv cache is set to default 48GB. we suspected the cache size but the eviction pattern looks like prefix reuse collisions.
[00:01:10] Liam: ok that helps. quick framing: our kv cache is prefix-keyed and uses LRU-with-weighting; heavy reuse of a small set of prefixes can create hot spots, but the more insidious is prefix collisions when different conversation ids share similar hash spaces — that can force eviction cycles.
[00:01:35] Maya: and there's also paging behavior when the cache can't hold the active kv set so the runtime spills to the node local SSD if configured, or to host swap if not. which do you have turned on?
[00:01:52] Selena: we had spillover to local SSD enabled, but ironically, once the SSD is saturated it starts serializing and that's when the 1s latencies show up. the telemetry shows heavy io wait.
[00:02:15] Marco: from a privacy angle, we want to confirm anything written to SSD is encrypted with our KMS keys.
[00:02:25] Liam: yes, the runtime respects host-level encryption and for private deployments we recommend using host-encrypted volumes + customer-managed KMS; i'll include the config snippet.
[00:02:38] [00:03:05] Ravi: one odd thing — when we pinned a few prefixes in a quick test, the eviction stopped for those flows but others got noisy and we still saw a background thrash every ~10 minutes. is that expected?
[00:03:25] Liam: yeah this sounds like prefix reuse anti-affinity got worse. pinning reduces eviction for those keys but increases pressure elsewhere; if total working set still exceeds available KV capacity you'll get periodic full-scan evictions.
[00:03:45] Maya: do we have prefetching enabled? sometimes prefetching of predicted next prefixes reduces miss rate but increases memory usage.
[00:03:57] Selena: we turned prefetch on in staging (prefetch window 2) but turned off in prod because of memory.
[00:04:12] Liam: worth instrumenting: prefetching can help when your sequence of prefixes is predictable, but in chatty multi-session workloads it can actually amplify spillover.
[00:04:34] [00:05:00] Ravi: another dimension is batching. we're using relatively small micro-batches per GPU to maintain low p99; does batching affect kv hits?
[00:05:15] Liam: yes - batching changes token interleaving and can improve contiguous prefix reuse if you batch sessions by conversation affinity. the runtime supports affinity-aware batching but you need to configure session hashing and sharding appropriately.
[00:05:38] Maya: can you explain the affinity-aware batcher briefly?
[00:05:44] Liam: sure: instead of naive round-robin, we group requests that are likely to hit the same kv prefixes, that reduces churn in the cache and boosts hit rate. tradeoff is sometimes you get imbalanced batch sizes so latency SLOs must be watched.
[00:06:10] [00:06:40] Selena: question about quantization — we're running 8-bit quantized model variants on the dedicated pool. could quantized kernels change memory footprint of kv or affect eviction?
[00:06:55] Liam: quantization reduces model weight memory but KV cache size is largely dependent on activations and KV key/value sizes which are architecture-dependent. however some optimized kernels alter prefix tokenization or kv packing slightly which can change per-token kv size. uncommon but possible.
[00:07:20] Ravi: in our telemetry we saw a small (~5%) increase in kv entry size after switching to an 8-bit runtime build, which might explain the higher working set.
[00:07:35] Maya: good catch. we'll add that to the checklist — measure per-entry size pre/post-quant.
[00:07:50] [00:08:10] Ravi: ok let's walk through the trace i uploaded. the first attach is the evict trace — you'll see cyclical evictions starting at 02:12:30 into the run.
[00:08:22] Maya: link?
[00:08:24] Ravi: shared folder: https://drive.internal/aurora/kv-traces/2025-12-01-evict.zip (note: placeholder)
[00:08:36] Liam: i pulled the top-line — two observations: 1) a set of ~120 hot prefixes are 60% of lookups; 2) eviction floods correlate with background long-context jobs that stream many tokens and push the working set.
[00:08:58] [00:09:18] Selena: is it worthwhile to increase KV cache to 128GB? we have headroom in host ram but concerned about cost and diminishing returns.
[00:09:34] Liam: yes increasing cache reduces miss rate but you hit law of diminishing returns; we prefer to couple cache sizing with prefix affinity and batching fixes. there are also smarter eviction policies (e.g., LFU-with-aging) we can enable as a knob.
[00:09:56] Maya: note on policy: by default we use LRU-weighted but for mixed long/short contexts LFU-with-aging often reduces thrash.
[00:10:12] [00:10:40] Marco: from compliance perspective, if we enable LFU and prefetch, does that change what gets flushed to disk? we need to document retention.
[00:10:51] Liam: no change in retention semantics; eviction and spill behavior are orthogonal to retention. anything written to disk follows the same residency and encryption policies. i'll add a snippet for retention settings.
[00:11:10] [00:11:45] Ravi: okay, practical question — can we avoid SSD spillover entirely? we have fast NVMe but writes still block.
[00:11:58] Liam: you can avoid spill by enlarging kv in memory or by enabling aggressive prefix compaction (we can evict less-used KV fragments earlier). also we have a mode called "read-through cache" vs "write-through spill" — read-through avoids writes unless necessary. we'll show config.
[00:12:28] [00:12:55] Selena: show us the command or profile we should run to collect the kv histograms.
[00:13:05] Liam: i'll paste the sampling command in the follow-up note — it captures kv size hist, eviction timestamps, and per-prefix hit rates; it's lightweight.
[00:13:20] [00:13:50] Maya: let's talk about prefix collisions — how do collisions show up in telemetry?
[00:13:56] Liam: collisions usually appear as bursts of evictions for seemingly unrelated session ids but with overlapping hash buckets. you'll see a correlation matrix where distinct conv ids map to same prefix buckets and hit rates oscillate. sometimes namespacing prefixes (add tenant id or session salt) fixes it.
[00:14:28] Ravi: we do prefix hashing with default salt; maybe that's the issue — multi-tenant noise.
[00:14:35] Selena: we can add tenant scoping to prefix keying, but worry about increasing total kv footprint since namespacing will reduce sharing.
[00:14:51] Liam: correct — it's a tradeoff: isolating prefixes reduces collisions but increases effective working set. often tenant scoping + slightly bigger cache is better than leaving collisions.
[00:15:20] [00:15:50] Maya: can you walk through an example of the config patch to add tenant salt?
[00:15:58] Liam: yes, small patch: set kv.prefix_format to "tenant:{tenant_id}:conv:{conv_hash}" and enable prefix-truncation to avoid overly long keys; i'll include in runbook.
[00:16:28] [00:16:58] Selena: another question: our orchestration autoscaler sometimes moves pods and that invalidates local cache and causes cold starts — any recommendations?
[00:17:10] Liam: ideally, avoid pod preemption for cache-heavy nodes; for Dedicated you can pin pods to nodes with taints/tolerations or use stateful sets with local storage pinned. also use global warmup buckets so newly scheduled pods prefetch expected hot prefixes on startup.
[00:17:38] Ravi: so prefetch at startup is supported?
[00:17:43] Liam: yes, warmup prefetch lists can be provided via config or via API — we call it startup warm keys.
[00:17:56] [00:18:25] Maya: turning to telemetry — what fields should Aurora surface to help us triage?
[00:18:31] Liam: minimum set: per-prefix hit rate, per-prefix size, eviction timestamps, eviction reason codes (memory pressure vs collision), disk spill metrics (IO wait, bytes/sec), and batch affinity mapping.
[00:18:52] Selena: we have custom logging but need a standard schema to correlate with runtime traces.
[00:18:58] Liam: i'll send the telemetry schema; it includes example Grafana panels.
[00:19:20] [00:19:50] Ravi: small tangent — we saw some p99 spikes when quantized kernels used fused-atten ops; is that a KV issue or model kernel scheduling?
[00:20:05] Liam: likely kernel scheduling; fused kernels can create short bursts of GPU contention which then cascade into delayed KV writes. we should correlate GPU utilization with eviction windows.
[00:20:26] [00:20:52] Selena: logging shows GPU p95 ~= 80% during bursts, and then evictions spike once utilization crosses 85%.
[00:21:02] Liam: that matches an observed coupling: long-context token generation increases KV churn and GPU occupancy; if both climb together you get non-linear latency.
[00:21:25] [00:21:50] Maya: any quick fixes?
[00:21:55] Liam: short term: throttle long-context streaming jobs or place them on a separate capacity pool with bigger KV; medium term: affinity batching + increased KV + LFU-with-aging.
[00:22:12] [00:22:45] Ravi: question on the runtime's paging policy: it writes pinned segments first or least-recently-accessed?
[00:22:54] Liam: it writes LR-evict-first but you can tweak to write coldest segments first or pin hot segments. we also support moving cold to remote object store in a tiered fashion but that increases tail latency.
[00:23:20] [00:23:50] Selena: remote object store sounds risky for low latency workloads.
[00:23:55] Liam: yes it's a last-resort for very large context archives; not recommended for interactive SLOs.
[00:24:15] [00:24:45] Marco: privacy check — anything moved to remote store must be encrypted and key-managed by us.
[00:24:53] Liam: agreed. we provide hooks for client-side envelope encryption before tiering.
[00:25:12] [00:25:40] Maya: let's sketch a concrete experiment plan so we converge. propose three runs: baseline, pinned-prefix (small hot set), and affinity-batched with increased kv.
[00:25:54] Ravi: baseline is current config (48GB kv, prefetch off, default batching), pinned-prefix uses pinned list of 150 prefixes, affinity uses affinity-aware batching + kv=128GB.
[00:26:12] Selena: we'll also flip into 8-bit quant build vs current to measure per-entry size delta.
[00:26:22] Liam: great. capture GPU utl, kv hist, eviction trace. try to run each for 30 minutes to see steady state — but you can probably detect thrash in 10-15 minutes.
[00:26:42] [00:27:05] Maya: timeline?
[00:27:08] Ravi: we'll run in staging first, target runs by next Tue which is 2025-12-09.
[00:27:16] Maya: ok. Liam will send scripts and runbook by Friday 2025-12-05.
[00:27:30] [00:27:55] Selena: small operational ask: when evictions happen, can the runtime surface a list of prefixes evicted in the last N seconds as a single endpoint?
[00:28:07] Liam: yes, there's an endpoint /runtime/kv/recent-evicted that returns a top-K list and reason codes; we'll share API docs.
[00:28:22] Maya: we'll include that in the runbook.
[00:28:36] [00:29:00] Marco: compliance: please include audit logs for eviction API and who requested prefetch lists.
[00:29:10] Liam: eviction API calls are logged with service account and tenant id; retention defaults to 90 days but can be configured.
[00:29:26] [00:29:55] Ravi: gotcha. a few follow-ups: 1) can we change eviction policy without restart? 2) is there a graceful warmup?
[00:30:07] Liam: eviction policy can be toggled at runtime via config endpoint and is pushed to workers without full restart; warmup keys can be injected via API too.
[00:30:24] [00:30:50] Maya: nice. now a quick weirdness — on one run we saw the runtime reporting evicted prefixes but the eviction count didn't change, like double-counting?
[00:31:02] Liam: sounds like a telemetry dedupe bug — sometimes the telemetry aggregator duplicates events when a shard restarts. we'll look at the trace.
[00:31:20] [00:31:45] Selena: earlier you mentioned LFU aging — what's a safe default aging window?
[00:31:51] Liam: typical is 10-30 minutes depending on session length; for chatty low-latency workloads we lean towards 10 minutes.
[00:32:06] [00:32:30] Ravi: are there any runtime patches that would be quick wins? maybe increase hash buckets or change salt?
[00:32:38] Liam: increasing hash buckets reduces collision probability with negligible cost; change salt for tenant scoping is also quick. both are low risk.
[00:32:54] Maya: ok let's capture decisions: enable tenant scoping in staging, increase buckets, try LFU-aging=10m, re-run benchmarks.
[00:33:08] [00:33:40] Liam: side note on monitoring: set an alert on eviction rate > 1000/min or disk io wait > 20% for > 2m. that usually catches thrash early.
[00:33:58] Selena: we'll add those to our alerting.
[00:34:12] [00:34:40] Ravi: on the SSD encryption question — we currently have host LUKS + cloud KMS tied, but need to confirm runtime writes again respect KMS envelope; marco will verify.
[00:34:52] Marco: i'll validate the key wrap and share notes.
[00:35:06] [00:35:30] Maya: any other blockers?
[00:35:35] Ravi: maybe one more — we saw occasional GC pauses in the runtime process correlated with big writes to disk. are those in our control?
[00:35:45] Liam: GC tuning may help; the runtime is golang-based for control-plane components and has GC knobs; also avoid synchronous fsync on every write — we can batch writes to reduce GC pressure.
[00:36:05] [00:36:30] Selena: ok we'll include GC trace collection.
[00:36:40] [00:37:00] Maya: recap — Liam runs scripts + runbook by 2025-12-05; Aurora runs benchmarks by 2025-12-09; follow-up review 2025-12-11. send security and retention notes.
[00:37:18] Marco: noted.
[00:37:34] [00:38:00] Maya: any objections to Redwood providing a short config patch for Dedicated pools to bump KV to 96GB for a test window?
[00:38:12] Ravi: fine to test but will need cost estimate.
[00:38:20] Maya: i'll include cost note with the config patch.
[00:38:36] [00:38:58] Selena: unrelated but FYI we have periodic load tests that create a lot of ephemeral prefixes from downstream connectors; might need to add filter rules for them.
[00:39:12] Liam: good point — drop ephemeral connector prefixes from being cached or reduce their TTL.
[00:39:30] [00:40:00] Ravi: question on logs — the prefetched keys list we provided earlier, can it be versioned? we want to audit who changed warm lists.
[00:40:10] Liam: warm key APIs are auditable and versioned; we can show a history endpoint.
[00:40:26] [00:40:50] Maya: ok looks like we're aligned. any closing comments?
[00:40:58] Marco: just that we'll need the KMS confirmation before enabling SSD spill in prod.
[00:41:08] Liam: understood.
[00:41:20] Maya: great, thanks everyone. i'll follow up with notes and the recording.
[00:41:33] [END]

Notes on transcription: auto-transcribed, occasional mis-hearings (e.g., "kv cache" sometimes appears as "k v cash"), filler words not removed.
